Collatz

SequencesParityNumber Theory
Game: Follow a number as it changes again and again to see where it ends up; there is no winning or losing.
How to play: Type a starting number, choose how even numbers change, then press Next step or Show all. You can also tap the picture or use the arrow keys.

Tap the left of the picture to go back, the middle to step forward, or the right to show all. With the picture focused, use the arrow keys.

Even numbers
Step 0
Look for the math

Start at 27 and the numbers bounce up and down like hailstones before they settle into a small loop. Nobody has proved that every start settles down, which is why this is the famous Collatz conjecture and not a theorem. The original applet drew the whole path at once and offered a pop-up list; here you step through the same path and the list sits under the chart.

Even or odd

The rule depends only on parity: an even number is halved, an odd number becomes 3n + 1. The applet's multiplier is fixed at 3. Its "Divide by 2" setting (the default) takes out one factor of two per step; "Strip of 2" takes out every factor of two in a single step. Both settings keep going until a number repeats, which means a loop has been found. The original also had an "Autonomous digits" switch; this page always redraws at once, which was that switch's default.

The two loops

In "Divide by 2" mode the trail falls into the 3-cycle 4, 2, 1, 4. In "Strip of 2" mode it falls into the shorter 2-cycle 4, 1, 4. The numbers form an integer sequence: each value is worked out from the one before it. The logic test followed every start from 1 to 20,000 in both modes, allowing up to 1,000 steps, and found no other loop. The applet only allows 150 steps, so its trail for 703 stops before the loop closes. Try 8: divide mode goes 8, 4, 2, 1, while strip mode goes 8, 1.

How long is the ride?

Count the steps until a number first reaches 1. No start below 27 needs more than 100 steps, and 27 needs 111. The page then lists 27, 31, 41, 47, 55, 62 as "such numbers", but that list is only a sample: 54 and 63 also take more than 100 steps, and the test found them in the true order. This counting is a question in number theory. The applet gives up after 150 steps; 2,817 of the first 20,000 starts hit that cap, 703 being the first. A very large start can also outgrow the numbers this page holds exactly; the trail then stops with the applet's own "is problematic" message.

The cheaper rule

If an odd number uses (3n + 1)/2 instead, the trip is shorter. The poem on the original page says a $27 item first drops below $27 on day 59 and reaches the 2, 1 loop on day 69. With "Divide by 2" and "(3n + 1)/2" both on, the test found exactly that: step 59 gives 23 and step 69 gives 2. This is the economical form R. Terras used, in which an odd step already includes one halving.

Try 27 with "(3n + 1)/2" switched on, press Show all, and watch the loop appear at the end of the chart.
